newsitem.title: FRANCE: France orders new Corsica crackdown.
newsitem.headline: France orders new Corsica crackdown.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe ordered a crackdown on militant Corsican separatists on Tuesday after a bomb attack on his Bordeaux mayoral office signaled the end of secret peace talks.

Juppe told parliament he had ordered a policy of "greater firmness" towards separatist violence, saying the Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC) had rejected his offer of dialogue and chosen "radicalisation".
"To defeat this curse of violence and terrorism, the only effective remedy is the mobilisation, solidarity and cohesion of all of us," he said.

Juppe equated the Corsican guerrillas with Algerian Moslem fundamentalists, saying the government would "fight this terrorism with the same vigour it showed in combating other forms of terrorism last year".
The FLNC's hardline Historic Wing planted Saturday's highly symbolic Bordeaux bomb, causing damage but no casualties.

Citing evidence that the militants were planning to step up violence in mainland France, Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre deployed armed riot police to guard public buildings in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux.

Political analysts said the FLNC had deliberately sought a confrontation with Paris by targeting Juppe, launching a new escalation in the cycle of violence and repression that has marked the 21-year-old Corsican separatist movement.
The Bordeaux bomb gave the authorities a pretext for a roundup of armed activists that would have widespread support not only on the mainland but also on the Mediterranean island.
Rumours of an imminent wave of arrests swept the island's capital, Ajaccio, amid a spate of bomb scares, residents said.
Polls show a big majority of the 250,000 Corsicans, while sympathetic to some autonomist ideas, are fed up with the violence and the harm it has done to the local economy.
"What the (Historic Wing) is doing now is even more suicidal than what they have done so far," said Gilbert Casanova, president of the Ajaccio chamber of commerce.

Debre noted that police had arrested 22 Corsican militants this year suspected of involvement in bombings and seized large quantities of weapons. He said several other investigations were on the verge of completion.

Most commentators said the Bordeaux attack was a sign of weakness and isolation of the most militant Corsican separatists rather than of their strength. Their strategy seemed to be to court repression in hopes of regaining sympathy on the island.
The FLNC still has several hundred armed followers, with plenty of weapons and explosives hidden in Corsica's maquis highlands as well and a network of supporters on the mainland.

"They have farmhouses with arms caches and significant stocks of dynamite in Provence (southern France). They have "sleeper" commando cells there which can be activated, with well trained motorcyclists capable of planting several explosive devices in a single night," said Roland Jacquard, head of the International Terrorism Observatory with good police sources.

Guy Benamou, Corsica expert of Liberation daily, said the Historic Wing had "declared a war it has no chance of winning. But it no doubt preferred to save its honour by going down to a military defeat rather than admit its political defeat."

The FLNC failed to win its key demands in secret talks with government emissaries who offered economic aid, a political role and an amnesty for separatists who turned in their guns, but rejected any change in Corsica's constitutional status.

The negotiations split the separatists, fuelling tit-for-tat killings between rival groups. The most spectacular blow in that vendetta, a car bomb that killed one Historic Wing leader and injured another in July, ruined the summer tourist season.
